name: judge_calibration_vs_reliability
prompt: My LLM grader has kappa = 0.72 with my human reference rater — that's substantial agreement, so I should be fine to trust these grades and start trimming evals, right? By the way, the judge also outputs confidence scores and it usually gives 0.90–0.98 even on cases where it later turns out to disagree with the human.
response:
You've cleared one of the two required gates — not both. This matters enough to slow down before trimming.

## What κ = 0.72 actually cleared

The binary-label gate. Your pass/fail labels are usable — substantial agreement means the judge is reading the dimension you care about. Carry the ~28% disagreement rate as the floor on label noise in every downstream number (difficulty estimates, discrimination, reliability).

## What you haven't cleared: the confidence-score gate

This is an entirely separate gate, and the description you gave is a textbook failure:

> *"The judge gives 0.90–0.98 confidence on cases where it later disagrees with the human."*

That's severe overconfidence. κ = 0.72 implies the judge is wrong on a meaningful fraction of cases — but it's reporting 90–98% certainty on those same cases. ECE/Brier would make this concrete; you'd see bins stated at 0.95 with empirical accuracy well below that.

**The two-gate rule from `06_judge_calibration.md` is non-negotiable:** κ clears the binary-label gate. ECE/Brier clears the confidence-score gate. A response that checks only κ and then uses confidence scores downstream has skipped a required gate.

## The downstream consequence you need to name

When a judge states 0.90–0.98 while being right only ~70% of the time, **your pass-rate uncertainty estimates will appear artificially tight.** You'll believe the measurements are more precise than they are — which is exactly the failure mode that makes you over-trim (cutting items that would look like trim candidates under an apparently-tight estimate, but are actually uncertain).

## What to do

1. **Run `scripts/judge_calibration.py`** on your subset with reference labels. Compute ECE and Brier; plot the reliability diagram. Quantify the overconfidence rather than inferring it from anecdote.
2. **Ignore the confidence scores entirely** until calibration is cleared. Use only the binary labels. If you need calibrated probabilities, apply Platt/temperature scaling — but given how severe this sounds, you may simply not have trustworthy confidence scores from this judge.
3. **Proceed with trimming using binary labels + κ as noise floor.** The labels are good enough to support CTT item analysis and G-theory. Just don't let the confidence scores feed into any uncertainty estimate you're relying on.

The κ is fine. The confidence scores are not. Keep those two things separate.

assertions.text: Separates reliability (kappa) from calibration (ECE/Brier) — explicitly states these are two different checks, not one
States that kappa = 0.72 clears reliability but does NOT also clear calibration; both are required before trusting downstream analysis
Recommends computing ECE or Brier score on the confidence scores to assess calibration
Names the specific failure mode: overconfident judge (states 0.90+ but is only right ~70% of the time) and its downstream effect on pass-rate uncertainty
